extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on evaluating prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102/103, including determination of anticipation vs obviousness, operability/enablement of references, public use/on-sale issues, drawings as prior art, and treatment of tax-strategy limitations under the AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102 the claim is anticipated by the reference (no question of obviousness); the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention explicitly or implicitly (features not directly taught must be inherently present). Under 35 U.S.C. 103 the reference teachings must be modified to meet the claims and the modification must have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art as of the relevant time (effective filing date for AIA, time of invention for pre-AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep distinction in mind when making rejections; see MPEP §§ 2131-2146 and 2150-2159.04 for guidance on patentability determinations under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting proper 35 U.S.C. 102 paragraph (AIA vs pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a printed publication or patent is found to disclose the claimed invention, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) (AIA) or under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the effective filing date of the claimed invention (see MPEP § 2139.01 for pre-AIA and MPEP § 2152.01 for AIA) and the issue/publication date of the reference (see MPEP §§ 2124, 2126, 2128-2128.02, and 2152.02-2154.02(c)). See MPEP § 2152.05 for whether to apply 102(a)(1) or (a)(2). Use form paragraph 7.03.aia or 7.03.fti in Office actions to indicate which regime applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection by persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art or by amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art. Additional ways to overcome depend on whether claims are subject to the AIA first-inventor-to-file provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2152.06 for overcoming rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2); see MPEP §§ 2132.01, 2133.02(a), and 2136.05 et seq. for overcoming pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), and (e) rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use, on-sale activity, or knowledge as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use, sale of the invention, or knowledge of the invention by others may preclude patentability under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) (AIA) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b), depending on the facts and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If activity is by an entity other than the inventors/assignee, both pre-AIA 102(a) and (b) may apply. If evidence only points to knowledge within the year prior to the effective filing date then pre-AIA 102(a) applies; however, do not make a pre-AIA 102(a) rejection if evidence shows applicant made the invention and only disclosed it within the one-year grace period. Examiner may require applicant to answer specific questions (35 U.S.C.132 and 37 CFR 1.104(a)(2)); consider requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 where reasonably necessary (see MPEP § 704.10 et seq.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for information on public use or sale (form paragraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an issue of public use, on-sale activity, or other public availability is raised, the examiner may issue a requirement for additional information from applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.104.aia for AIA cases or 7.104.fti for pre-AIA cases; such a requirement must be preceded by form paragraph 7.105 and may be followed by form paragraphs 7.122–7.126 as appropriate. Information sought should be restricted to what is reasonably necessary (see MPEP § 2133.03). Set a two-month reply period unless the Office action has a shortened statutory period (SSP); failure to reply timely results in abandonment (35 U.S.C. 133). If sufficient evidence exists to establish a prima facie case, use form paragraph 7.16.aia or 7.16.fti to make the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that prior art references are operable/enabling
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference expressly anticipates or makes obvious all elements of the claimed invention, the reference is presumed to be operable. Once such a reference is found, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the presumption of operability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Sasse and In re Antor Media Corp. support this presumption. An examiner making a proper prima facie case of anticipation need not conduct an inquiry into whether the prior art is enabling; applicant must submit rebuttal evidence of nonenablement. See MPEP § 716.07 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure standard is the same regardless of prior art type
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of disclosure required within a reference to make it an 'enabling disclosure' is the same whether the reference is a U.S. patent, foreign patent, printed publication, or other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no statutory basis to discriminate among prior art on nationality or type. See In re Moreton and MPEP § 2121 for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of efficacy not required for prior art enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference provides an enabling disclosure if it describes the invention in sufficient detail to enable one of ordinary skill to carry out the claimed invention; proof of efficacy is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Impax Labs. Inc. v. Aventis Pharm. Inc. (proof of efficacy not required for anticipation). See MPEP § 2122 for discussion of utility in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using secondary evidence to show a primary reference is operable (for 35 U.S.C. 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the primary reference does not itself teach how to practice the invention, a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection is possible if secondary evidence (other patents/publications) shows public possession of the method of making or using the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite secondary references to establish an enabling disclosure by the primary reference (In re Donohue). See MPEP § 2131.01 for more information on using secondary references to show enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inoperative/non-enabling prior art in 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-enabling or inoperative reference may still qualify as prior art for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Beckman Instruments v. LKB Produkter AB; Symbol Techs. Inc. v. Opticon Inc. Use such references for 103 analyses even if they are inoperative for anticipation purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds/compositions enabling requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For chemical compounds/compositions, one of ordinary skill in the art must be able to make or synthesize the claimed compound from the disclosure; mere naming of a compound without more cannot constitute a description if a process for making was not known at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is presumed operable until applicant rebuts that presumption (In re Sasse). Applicant must provide evidence showing that a process for making the compound was not known at the time of the invention. See MPEP § 2121.02 for evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsuccessful attempts to make compounds before the date of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If attempts to prepare a disclosed compound or composition were unsuccessful before the date of invention, the reference does not contain an 'enabling disclosure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of unsuccessful prior attempts can show inoperability (In re Wiggins). However, mere fact that an author did not attempt synthesis without more may be insufficient to overcome a rejection (In re Donohue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant-related enablement (growing/cultivating requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are drawn to plants, the reference combined with prior art knowledge must enable one of ordinary skill to reproduce the plant (i.e., grow/cultivate it); pictures alone may be insufficient if key grafting or propagation information is missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re LeGrice (rose pictures insufficient), Ex parte Thomson (commercial seed availability may make disclosure enabling), In re Elsner (combination of publication identifying plant + foreign sale + asexual reproducibility can create a statutory bar). See MPEP § 2152.02(d) for foreign sales under AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures/drawings may constitute enabling disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured and may be used to reject claims to the article if the picture shows all the claimed structural features and how they are put together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origin of the drawing is immaterial; drawings in design or utility patents can anticipate or render obvious. Evaluate drawings for what they reasonably disclose to one of ordinary skill (In re Bager; Jockmus v. Leviton; In re Mraz; In re Aslanian). Proportions in drawings not to scale have little evidentiary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility not required to be disclosed in a reference for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference must identically disclose the claimed compound for anticipation, but it need not disclose a utility for the compound; no utility disclosure is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: In re Schoenwald and related discussion in MPEP § 2122. A claimed compound may be anticipated even if the reference does not disclose a use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpreferred/alternative embodiments are prior art; teaching away not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosed examples and preferred embodiments do not teach away from a broader disclosure or nonpreferred embodiments. Disclosure of alternatives does not constitute teaching away merely because some alternatives are labeled inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Susi, In re Gurley (teaching away insufficient if no discovery beyond known art), In re Fulton (mere disclosure of alternatives is not teaching away). Prior art may be relied upon for all it reasonably suggests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception: post-filing factual references may be used in limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: In some circumstances, factual references that postdate the filing may be cited to show universal facts (e.g., that undue experimentation would have been required, that a parameter was or was not critical, or that a statement in the specification is inaccurate), but post-effective-filing-date evidence cannot be used to determine whether the application is enabled or described under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Wilson, In re Corneil, In re Rainer, In re Marzocchi, In re Langer, In re Glass, and Amgen Inc. v. Sanofi for the limits and permissible uses of later factual evidence. Post-effective-filing-date evidence is improper to illuminate post-filing state-of-the-art for enablement/written-description determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax strategies deemed within the prior art (AIA §14 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AIA section 14, any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability ('tax strategy') shall be deemed to be within the prior art for purposes of novelty and nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103; applicants cannot rely on novelty/non-obviousness of a tax strategy to distinguish claims from prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two exclusions: (1) parts of inventions used solely for preparing a tax or information return (including recording/transmitting/organizing data related to such filing) and (2) parts used solely for financial management to the extent severable from any tax strategy. This provision applies to applications/patents pending, filed, or issued on or after Sept. 16, 2011. Follow the examination procedure: (1) construe claim (MPEP § 2111 et seq.), (2) analyze 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112, (3) identify limitations relating to a tax strategy and note exclusions, (4) evaluate the claim under 102/103 treating tax-strategy limitations as prior art. Form paragraph 7.06.01 may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of computer-implemented methods vis-à-vis tax-strategy provision
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuinely novel and non-obvious computer-implemented method for manipulating data is not affected by the tax-strategy provision merely because it is used for a tax purpose; however, a prior-art computer-implemented method does not become non-obvious simply by implementing a novel tax strategy. Claim limitations solely enabling filing of income tax returns or assisting with managing finances should be given patentable weight, except limitations directed to a tax strategy should not be given patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the four-step examination guidance for tax strategies and consider whether claimed computer-implemented features are severable from tax-strategy limitations.
